content:
The [MAC Address Generator](/mac-address-generator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Generate random MAC addresses — locally administered, unicast, in your format. Enter your how many addresses and format and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Generate random MAC addresses for testing, documentation and network configuration. Every address is locally administered (the second hex digit of the first octet is 2, 6, A or E) and unicast, which is what you want for a made-up address: it can never collide with a manufacturer's real address range. Addresses are generated with the browser's cryptographic random source and never leave your device — nothing here is sent to a server. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the MAC Address Generator

Start by entering your how many addresses, then choosing your format from the list. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Choose how many addresses you need — up to 20 at a time.
2. Pick the format: colons, dashes or plain hex.
3. Copy the addresses from the result — change the count to generate a fresh set.

## Formula

Six random octets; the first octet has its multicast bit cleared and its locally-administered bit set ((byte & 0xFE) | 0x02), so the second hex digit is 2, 6, A or E.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [MAC Address Generator](/mac-address-generator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. Six addresses in colon format look like 02:4F:A1:9C:3E:77, 06:11:8B:2D:F0:4A and so on — each one random, each one locally administered, and no two the same. Try the same figures in the [MAC Address Generator](/mac-address-generator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (How many addresses: 6, Format: Colon separated (AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF)), the [MAC Address Generator](/mac-address-generator) returns MAC addresses: 1E:AA:6F:25:6D:2D EE:A8:8C:06:5A:09 FE:79:16:CC:8B:D5 BE:C6:D2:B0:72:92 72:8E:C1:2F:B3:A3 52:2D:18:86:D9:37, Count: 6, Type: Locally administered, unicast. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. ## Locally administered vs universal

A MAC address is 48 bits: the first 24 are the manufacturer's OUI and the last 24 are the device's serial. The second-least-significant bit of the first octet marks the address as locally administered when it is 1 — the address was assigned by software, not burned in by a manufacturer. Random generators always set that bit, because a random address with it clear could accidentally duplicate a real device's address on the same network.

## Unicast vs multicast

The least significant bit of the first octet marks multicast: 1 means the address is a group address, 0 means it belongs to a single device. This generator always clears it, so every address it makes is a unicast address — the kind a single network card has.

## When to use a random MAC address

Random MACs are used for testing network software, writing documentation, configuring virtual machines, and for MAC randomisation — a privacy feature in modern phones and laptops that rotates the address a device shows to each Wi-Fi network. Never use a random MAC to impersonate another device on a network you do not own.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- Generated addresses are locally administered — they can never clash with a real manufacturer's range.
- Colon format is the most common; Cisco devices often use dots, and plain hex suits config files.
- Need more than 20? Generate in batches — every batch is independently random.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a MAC address?

A 48-bit hardware identifier for a network device, written as six pairs of hex digits (for example 02:4F:A1:9C:3E:77). It identifies the device on its local network. Try it with your own numbers in the [MAC Address Generator](/mac-address-generator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Are these MAC addresses safe to use?

They are locally administered unicast addresses, which means they cannot collide with any manufacturer's real address range. They are fine for testing, VMs and documentation. Try it with your own numbers in the [MAC Address Generator](/mac-address-generator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What does locally administered mean?

It means the address was assigned by software rather than burned in by a manufacturer. The second hex digit of the first octet (2, 6, A or E) marks it, and this generator sets it on every address. Try it with your own numbers in the [MAC Address Generator](/mac-address-generator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the MAC Address Generator use?

Six random octets; the first octet has its multicast bit cleared and its locally-administered bit set ((byte & 0xFE) | 0x02), so the second hex digit is 2, 6, A or E. You can see it in action in the [MAC Address Generator](/mac-address-generator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
